articles.title: The Dark Side of Virtual Governance: Customer Perceived Knowledge Hiding and Relational Conflict in Customer Relationship Management Systems
articles.abstract: Retail applications have become the key means for most online retailers to manage customer relationships. However, the possible dark side of this virtual customer relationship governance has rarely been examined. By drawing on coping theory, this study investigates the negative customer communication experience of virtual governance in the context of online post-sales services. Customers’ perceived knowledge hiding is investigated as a mediator, while customers’ fear of opportunism and product knowledge are introduced as moderators. Data is collected from 302 Chinese online consumers and analyzed using PLS-SEM. The results show that in the post-sales service context, virtual governance increases the degree of relational conflict between customers and service providers through the mediation of customer perceived knowledge. In addition, customer product knowledge positively moderates the relationship between virtual governance and perceived knowledge hiding. These findings thus integrate different literature streams, improve the understanding of the application of virtual governance in the online post-sales service context, and expand the boundaries of relevant research.

articles.title: Boundary-Spanning Roles of University Public Information Officers Addressing the Demands of a Right to Information Act
articles.abstract: In 2013, the provincial government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) passed a Right to Information (RTI) Act. Government bodies, including public sector universities, were required to enforce the new law within four months of its enactment. A significant step in the implementation of the law was the appointment of Public Information Officers (PIOs). These were given the responsibility of ensuring that the communities served by the organization they represented could benefit from the new freedoms outlined under the RTI Act. This article reports on the findings of a series of interviews with the PIOs at 25 universities in KP. Transcripts of the interviews were subjected to a reflexive thematic analysis. The emergent theme that most related to the question of how PIOs in KP universities enact their roles under the RTI Act was that of boundary-spanning. In order to make information not only available but meaningful beyond the boundaries of their university, PIOs must act in seven boundary-spanning capacities: Officiator; Leadership in Information Synthesis; Linchpin; Accredited Representative; Information Intermediary; Cultural Ambassador; Mediator. These seven roles are described and discussed.

articles.title: Developing and Validating a Comprehensive Assessment Tool for Learning Commons in University Libraries: A Confirmatory Factor Analysis Approach
articles.abstract: Learning Commons have become integral to university libraries, necessitating robust assessment tools to evaluate their effectiveness. This study developed and validated a comprehensive assessment tool for Learning Commons in university libraries. Building on a systematic review of recent literature, a questionnaire was developed encompassing nine key constructs: Layout, Amenities, Atmosphere, Functionality, Flexible Learning Spaces, Technology Integration, Information Resources, Expert Support Services, and Collaborative Learning Spaces. The questionnaire underwent rigorous content validity assessment, followed by exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses using a sample of 500 university students. Results demonstrated excellent psychometric properties, with high reliability (Cronbach’s alpha ranging from 0.977 to 0.981) and strong content validity (CVI = 0.98, CVR = 0.92). Exploratory factor analysis revealed a clear nine-factor structure, with factor loadings ranging from 0.419 to 0.801. Confirmatory factor analysis supported this structure, with factor loadings ranging from 0.316 to 0.513 and excellent model fit indices (CFI = 0.987, TLI = 0.976, RMSEA = 0.048). This study contributes a valid and reliable instrument for comprehensively assessing Learning Commons, addressing a significant gap in the field. The developed tool enables evidence-based decision-making in designing, implementing, and improving Learning Commons in university libraries, with implications for enhancing student learning experiences and outcomes.

articles.title: Ontology and General Theory: Toward Library Science as a Science
articles.abstract: This paper asks: Can Library Science be a science? In response, it answers “yes” and illuminates how by integrating three sets of ideas–the phenomena addressed by Library Science, ontology identifying these phenomena, and theory about them. This integration illuminates a direction toward developing a scientific general theory of Library Science, one based upon ontology, that could depict, define, predict, and explain the phenomena of Library Science, especially as they occur through organizational librarianship occurring within organizations dedicated to librarianship, known as libraries. This ontology and its derived direction toward general theory encompasses several sets of Library Science phenomena: such organizational librarianship, especially its central phenomena; phenomena supporting and governing organizational librarianship’s central phenomena; as well as contextual phenomena generating and affected by organizational librarianship. The ontology and derived theoretical direction also identify the relationships governing these phenomena. These include causal relationships, ones arising from the dynamics among Library Science’s phenomena, and ones inherent to the phenomena’s ontology.

articles.title: Big Data, Bigger Stories? The Journey from Data to Impact in Public Libraries
articles.abstract: Data storytelling serves as a powerful tool for public libraries to move from measurement to demonstrating impact. This article reports findings from an exploratory focus group conducted at the Austin Public Library followed by individual interviews with 11 staff members from six large urban public library systems. The data demonstrates that libraries have made progress in data management and public narrative, particularly in short-term goals such as data-informed decision-making, promoting special programs, or securing funding. But the data also indicates that public libraries have room to grow in terms of identifying and articulating main narratives that define the library’s mission and long-term value. These main narratives are critical for guiding internal operations and strengthening connections with the external communities that public libraries serve. Public libraries are still facing a long journey from big data to bigger and more impactful stories. The data from these librarians offers broader insights for the field about how to translate data into narratives that demonstrate how public libraries work to serve the public good.

articles.title: Beyond Traditional Academia: Understanding Alternative-Academic Careers in the Chinese LIS Doctoral Job Market
articles.abstract: This study analyzes China’s library and information science (LIS) doctoral job market through the lens of alternative-academic (alt-ac) careers. Using a mixed-methods approach, we analysed 12,560 doctoral-level job postings from 607 institutions (2016–2024) with a BERT-BiLSTM-CRF model for entity recognition, followed by social network analysis. We identified four distinct alt-ac clusters – digital transformation, knowledge services, strategic intelligence, and cultural heritage – each demonstrating distinct evolution patterns. Network analysis revealed critical bridging roles, particularly data curation and subject librarians, that connect traditional academic functions with emerging professional domains. We developed a theoretical model explaining how alt-ac careers evolve through niche construction, knowledge brokering, and adaptive evolution mechanisms. Our findings suggest that alt-ac pathways function as complementary rather than alternative trajectories in the academic ecosystem. These findings inform doctoral education reform and labor market policy as China’s information landscape undergoes rapid digital transformation.
